title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin
sourceAuthor: Robert Browning; illustrated by Kate Greenaway
note: A condensed prose reading of Browning’s public-domain poem, retaining its sequence, principal details, and somber ending. The conversion from verse to prose, compression, and page divisions are editorial. The three illustrations are Kate Greenaway plates (images/img21.jpg, img20.jpg, and img38.jpg) from the cited edition. The German title is the conventional name of the Hamelin legend.

rights.basis: Project Gutenberg identifies ebook 18343, including Browning’s text and Greenaway’s illustrations, as public domain in the United States.

artLabel: The strange piper stands before Hamelin’s crowded roofs.

pageArt.alt: The Piper returns to Hamelin’s council after completing his work.
The town’s children follow the Piper away from Hamelin.

scenes: Hamelin town was overrun with rats. They fought the dogs, killed the cats, bit babies, spoiled the soup, and nested in hats. At last the people crowded into the town hall and demanded that the mayor and council find a remedy.

A stranger entered, tall and thin, wearing a coat half red and half yellow. He called himself a piper and said that, by a secret charm, he could free the town of every rat. The mayor promised him a thousand guilders when the work was done.

The Piper stepped into the street and played three shrill notes. From every house the rats came tumbling—great rats, small rats, old rats, and young. They followed him through the town to the river Weser, where all but one plunged in and drowned.

When the Piper returned for his money, the mayor offered only fifty guilders. The danger was gone, and the council laughed at his threat. The Piper warned them once, then put his pipe to his lips again.

This time the music drew the children from their games. Laughing and dancing, they followed the Piper out of Hamelin. A mountainside opened and closed behind them. Only a lame child remained, unable to keep pace, grieving that he had missed the joyous country the music promised. Hamelin never recovered its children, and the town remembered the price of a broken promise.
